title: Why Spark, Its Trade-offs, and the Driver, Executor and Cluster Manager Roles

concepts.heading: Advantages of Spark
concepts.body: Spark is a unified engine for large-scale data processing. One engine and one set of high-level APIs in Python, Scala, Java and R cover batch SQL, streaming, machine learning and graphs, so a team does not stitch several systems together. Its main speed advantage over disk-based MapReduce is that executors can keep a working dataset in memory between actions: a loop that reads the same data thirty times pays for the storage read once, then serves later passes from the cache. Spill to local disk keeps jobs running when data does not fit, so memory is an optimization rather than a requirement. Transformations are lazy, so the Catalyst optimizer sees the whole query and can prune columns, push filters down to the source and pick join strategies before any work starts. Lost partitions are rebuilt from lineage, the recorded chain of transformations, which gives fault tolerance without replicating every intermediate result. The same code runs on a laptop in local mode or on Kubernetes, YARN or a standalone cluster.

concepts.heading: Challenges of Spark
concepts.body: Spark is powerful but not free of cost. The most common trouble is the shuffle: wide operations such as joins on large tables, groupBy and distinct move data across the network and write shuffle files to disk, so they dominate runtime. Data skew makes one partition far larger than the rest, so one task keeps a whole stage waiting. Memory needs tuning, because executors can fail with out-of-memory errors or spend too much time in garbage collection, and a collect on a large result can exhaust the driver (spark.driver.maxResultSize defaults to 1g and aborts the job above it). Many tiny input files create many tiny tasks whose scheduling overhead exceeds the work. PySpark adds serialization between the JVM and Python worker processes when you use Python UDFs, which is why built-in functions are preferred. Finally, a distributed program is harder to debug than a single process: errors surface in executor logs, and lazy evaluation means a bug may appear far from the line that caused it.

concepts.heading: Driver, Executors and the Cluster Manager
concepts.body: A Spark application is a driver program plus executors. The driver runs your main function and creates the SparkSession (and the SparkContext inside it). It builds the plan, splits work into jobs, stages and tasks, and schedules tasks on executors. Executors are processes launched on worker nodes that run tasks and keep cached data in memory or on disk; each application has its own executors, which stay up for the whole application and run tasks in several threads. The cluster manager is an external service that hands out resources: standalone, YARN or Kubernetes. Spark is agnostic to which one, as long as it can acquire executor processes. The driver must accept incoming connections from its executors for its whole lifetime, so it should be network addressable from the workers and run close to them. Because each application has separate executor JVMs, two applications cannot share data without writing it to external storage. The driver also serves the web UI, typically on port 4040.

concepts.heading: Cores, Memory and Task Slots
concepts.body: Resources are set per executor. spark.executor.cores is the number of cores per executor (the default is 1 on YARN and all available cores of the worker in standalone mode), and spark.executor.memory is the JVM heap (default 1g). Each task needs spark.task.cpus cores, default 1, so the tasks that run at once in an executor equal executor cores divided by task cpus, rounded down. Total parallelism is executors times that number: 4 executors with 5 cores and one cpu per task give 20 task slots. A stage with 100 tasks then runs in five waves. Executor memory is not all usable for data: spark.memory.fraction (default 0.6) of heap minus 300 MB is shared by execution and storage, and spark.memory.storageFraction (default 0.5) of that region is immune to eviction by execution. For PySpark and other off-heap use, spark.executor.memoryOverhead adds non-heap memory, 10 percent of executor memory by default. Driver memory is spark.driver.memory, also 1g by default, and in client mode it must be set through spark-submit rather than in code.

examPoints: The driver builds the plan and schedules tasks; executors run tasks and hold cached data; the cluster manager only allocates resources.
Task slots = executors x floor(executor cores / spark.task.cpus); a 100-task stage on 20 slots runs in 5 waves.
Shuffles, skew, tiny files and Python UDF serialization are the usual challenges; in-memory reuse and lazy optimization are the advantages.

quiz.q: A job on 6 executors, each with 4 cores and the default spark.task.cpus, has a stage of 120 tasks of equal length. How many waves of tasks does that stage need?
choices: 4 waves, because 24 slots are used four times for the first 96 tasks and the rest follow
5 waves, because each of the 24 slots runs five tasks in turn
6 waves, because there are 6 executors and each takes its share one after another
30 waves, because only one task runs on an executor at any moment
quiz.explain: Slots = 6 x floor(4 / 1) = 24, and 120 / 24 = 5 waves. Executors run tasks in several threads, so one task per executor is wrong, and the number of executors alone does not set the wave count.

quiz.q: Which process requests executors from YARN or Kubernetes, sends tasks to them and, in client mode, runs in the process that submitted the application?
choices: The executor, which asks the cluster manager for more peers when work arrives
The cluster manager, which also compiles the user code into a plan
The driver, which owns the SparkSession and schedules the tasks
The worker node, which assigns tasks to executors on a schedule
quiz.explain: The driver holds the SparkSession, builds the plan and schedules tasks; with the cluster manager it acquires executors. The cluster manager only allocates resources, and executors only run tasks and store data. Deploy mode decides whether the driver runs outside the cluster (client) or inside it (cluster).

recap: Spark wins through one engine, in-memory reuse, lazy optimization and lineage-based recovery, and loses time to shuffles, skew, tiny files, memory limits and Python serialization. The driver plans and schedules, the cluster manager hands out resources, and executors with cores and memory run the tasks.

title: DataFrame and Dataset, the SparkSession Lifecycle, Caching and the Job-Stage-Task Hierarchy

concepts.heading: DataFrame versus Dataset
concepts.body: A Dataset is a distributed collection with strong typing and lambda functions, built on Spark SQL's optimized engine. The Dataset API exists in Scala and Java only; Python has no Dataset API. A DataFrame is a Dataset organized into named columns, like a table. In Scala and Java it is a Dataset of Row objects, and in Python (and R) it is the only structured API you have. For a PySpark developer the practical answer is therefore always DataFrame. The main benefit of the typed Dataset is that a mistyped field fails at compile time in Scala or Java; a DataFrame checks column names and types when the query is analyzed, at runtime. Both go through the same Catalyst optimizer and execution engine, so a DataFrame query is not slower than the equivalent Dataset query when you use column expressions. The older RDD API sits below both and offers no query optimization, which is why DataFrames are preferred. SQL, DataFrame and Dataset code produce the same kind of logical plan, so you can mix them in one program.

concepts.heading: The SparkSession Lifecycle
concepts.body: SparkSession is the entry point to DataFrame and SQL functionality. You build one with SparkSession.builder, optionally set appName and config values, and call getOrCreate(). That call returns the existing global default session if a valid one exists, otherwise it creates a new session and makes it the global default, so calling it twice does not start two engines. In pyspark shells and notebooks a session named spark already exists. Configuration set on the builder applies when the underlying SparkContext starts; runtime SQL settings can be changed afterwards with spark.conf.set. Deploy-level settings such as spark.driver.memory in client mode cannot be changed from code. newSession() returns a session with its own SQL configuration, temporary views and UDFs but the same SparkContext and table cache, which is how isolated sessions share a cluster. spark.stop() stops the underlying SparkContext; after that the application's executors are released and DataFrames from that session can no longer run jobs. Stop the session when the application is finished, not after each query.

concepts.heading: Caching, Storage Levels and Garbage Collection
concepts.body: Because transformations are lazy, a DataFrame used by several actions is recomputed from its source each time unless you persist it. df.cache() is shorthand for persist() with the default storage level, MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER for DataFrames (changed from memory-only in 3.0). The cache is lazy: nothing is stored until the first action materializes the partitions. Levels in PySpark include MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK, DISK_ONLY and replicated variants ending in _2; Python data is always pickled when stored as objects, so the serialized levels are Java and Scala options. Spark evicts old partitions in least-recently-used order, and unpersist() releases the cache early. Cached partitions that no longer fit in memory are recomputed under MEMORY_ONLY, or written to disk under MEMORY_AND_DISK. Garbage collection cost grows with the number of Java objects, so large caches of deserialized objects can cause long GC pauses; serialized storage or fewer, larger objects lowers it. If old-generation memory fills up, lower spark.memory.fraction so less is cached. Since Spark 4.0 the default JDK is 17 with the G1 collector.

concepts.heading: Jobs, Stages and Tasks
concepts.body: The execution hierarchy has four levels. An application is the driver plus its executors. Each action, such as count, collect or a write, spawns a job. Spark divides each job into stages at shuffle boundaries: operations that need no data movement between partitions (select, filter, withColumn, map-style work) are narrow and are pipelined inside one stage, while a wide operation such as groupBy, a sort-merge join or repartition ends a stage because data must be redistributed. A stage is a set of tasks that depend on earlier stages. A task is the smallest unit of work: it processes one partition and is sent to one executor. A stage therefore has as many tasks as its input has partitions. So df.groupBy('k').count().collect() is one job, normally two stages (the scan with partial aggregation, then the final aggregation after the shuffle), and as many tasks per stage as partitions. The Jobs, Stages and Storage tabs of the web UI show exactly this tree. Two actions on the same DataFrame make two jobs.

examPoints: Python has no Dataset API: in PySpark a DataFrame is the structured API; Scala and Java DataFrames are Dataset[Row].
cache() uses MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER for DataFrames and is lazy; unpersist() frees it, otherwise eviction is least-recently-used.
One action = one job; a shuffle ends a stage; one task processes one partition.

quiz.q: A PySpark developer calls df.cache() and then df.count() and df.show(). Which statement describes what happens?
choices: cache() immediately reads all data into memory, so the count job is not needed
The first action materializes the cache with the default level MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER; later actions read the cached partitions
Both actions recompute the data from the source because cache() has no effect without an explicit StorageLevel
The cache is stored only on the driver so that show() can print it without executors
quiz.explain: cache() only marks the DataFrame; the first action computes and stores the partitions, and later actions reuse them. It does not need an explicit level, and partitions live on executors, not on the driver.

quiz.q: A job runs df.filter(...).groupBy('k').agg(...).write.parquet(path). How many jobs and how many stages does Spark normally create?
choices: 1 job and 2 stages, because the groupBy shuffle ends the first stage
2 jobs and 2 stages, because the filter and the aggregation each trigger a job
1 job and 1 stage, because only wide operations create new jobs
3 jobs and 3 stages, because the filter, the aggregation and the write are separate actions
quiz.explain: Only the write is an action, so there is one job; the groupBy shuffle splits it into a map-side stage and a final stage. Filter is a narrow transformation and starts no job.

recap: DataFrame is the structured API in PySpark; getOrCreate() returns the one default session and spark.stop() ends the SparkContext. Cache is lazy, defaults to MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER and is evicted least-recently-used. Each action is a job, shuffles split jobs into stages, and each task works on one partition.

title: Partitions and Shuffles, Lazy Evaluation, and the Spark Modules

concepts.heading: Partitions and Shuffles
concepts.body: A partition is a slice of a dataset that one task processes, so the partition count sets the parallelism. When Spark reads files it packs data into partitions of up to spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, 128 MB by default. A shuffle redistributes data across the cluster so that rows with the same key meet; it is triggered by groupBy, most joins, distinct, orderBy and repartition. The map side writes shuffle files to local disk and the reduce side fetches them over the network. The number of output partitions of a DataFrame shuffle is spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, default 200. Adaptive Query Execution (on by default since 3.2) can coalesce those shuffle partitions at runtime, using an advisory size of 64 MB, so the final count may be lower than 200. repartition(n) always shuffles and can increase or decrease the count; coalesce(n) only merges existing partitions without a full shuffle, and if you request more than the current count it stays at the current count. The two differ in cost: coalesce is cheap but may leave uneven partitions.

concepts.heading: Transformations, Actions and Lazy Evaluation
concepts.body: Transformations create a new dataset from an existing one and are lazy: select, filter, withColumn, join, groupBy().agg() and orderBy only add a step to the plan. Actions force computation and return a result to the driver or write output: count, collect, show, take, first, and write operations such as df.write.parquet. This laziness lets Spark optimize the whole chain at once and avoid reading data that no action needs. Transformations are either narrow, where each output partition depends on one input partition (filter, select, map), or wide, where data crosses partitions through a shuffle (groupBy, join, distinct, repartition). Narrow steps are pipelined in a single stage. Since nothing runs until an action, errors in a bad column name show up at analysis time, but data-dependent errors show up only when an action runs. df.printSchema() and df.explain() are not actions: they read the plan, not the data. A DataFrame is also immutable; each transformation returns a new one and the original is unchanged.

concepts.heading: Reading Plans and Lineage
concepts.body: Spark records every DataFrame's lineage, the chain of transformations from the source. The driver turns your code into a logical plan, the Catalyst optimizer rewrites it (column pruning, predicate pushdown, constant folding), and a physical plan is chosen. df.explain() prints the physical plan, and explain('formatted') or explain(True) shows more detail. An Exchange node in the plan marks a shuffle and therefore a stage boundary; a BroadcastExchange marks a broadcast. If a partition is lost because an executor died, Spark recomputes only that partition by replaying the lineage, which is the basis of its fault tolerance. Long lineages are expensive to replay, so iterative loops sometimes truncate them with checkpointing or caching. Reading explain output is a core developer skill: look for Exchange to count shuffles, for PushedFilters to confirm that filters reach the file source, and for the join type, for example BroadcastHashJoin or SortMergeJoin.

concepts.heading: The Spark Modules
concepts.body: Spark Core provides the engine: scheduling, memory management, fault recovery and the RDD API. Spark SQL, with DataFrames and Datasets, is the module for structured data and the one used in most new code. Structured Streaming builds on it to process unbounded data with the same DataFrame operations. MLlib is the machine learning library; its DataFrame-based API lives in pyspark.ml, while the older RDD-based pyspark.mllib is in maintenance mode. The pandas API on Spark lets pandas-style code scale out on a cluster (import pyspark.pandas). GraphX handles graph processing. Spark Connect is a client-server layer that lets thin clients send DataFrame plans to a remote Spark server. A choice question usually reads like this: structured batch query is Spark SQL, an unbounded stream is Structured Streaming, scalable model training is pyspark.ml, and an existing pandas workflow that must scale is the pandas API on Spark. DStream-based Spark Streaming is the old API; Structured Streaming replaced it for new work.

examPoints: repartition(n) shuffles and can raise or lower the count; coalesce(n) only merges partitions without a full shuffle and cannot increase it.
Actions (count, collect, show, write) run jobs; transformations are lazy, and narrow ones pipeline in one stage while wide ones add a shuffle.
Pick the module from the workload: Spark SQL for tables, Structured Streaming for streams, pyspark.ml for models, pandas API on Spark for pandas code.

quiz.q: A DataFrame has 8 partitions. What does df.coalesce(16) return?
choices: A DataFrame with 16 partitions created by a full shuffle
A DataFrame with 8 partitions, because coalesce cannot increase the count
An error, because coalesce only accepts a smaller number than the current count
A DataFrame with 16 partitions made by splitting each existing partition without moving data
quiz.explain: coalesce is a narrow merge, and requesting more partitions than exist leaves the count unchanged. repartition(16) is the call that shuffles to a larger number.

quiz.q: A script builds df2 = df.filter('x > 5').select('x', 'y').withColumn('z', col('x') + 1) and then calls df2.printSchema(). How much data does Spark process at that point?
choices: The whole dataset, because filter must run before the schema is known
Only the rows where x is greater than 5, because the filter is applied during schema printing
The sample used for schema inference only, which is read from the source files
No data, because the steps are transformations and printSchema reads the plan, not the rows
quiz.explain: All three steps are lazy transformations, and printSchema is not an action; it reads the analyzed plan. Data is processed only when an action such as count or write runs.

recap: Partitions are the unit of parallelism; shuffles create new stages and default to 200 partitions that AQE may coalesce. repartition shuffles, coalesce only merges. Transformations are lazy and actions run jobs, with explain showing Exchange nodes. Choose Spark SQL, Structured Streaming, pyspark.ml or the pandas API on Spark by workload.

title: Reading and Writing with JDBC and Files, SQL on Files and Save Modes

concepts.heading: Reading and Writing Files
concepts.body: spark.read returns a DataFrameReader and df.write a DataFrameWriter. The generic form is spark.read.format('csv').option(...).load(path), and shortcuts such as spark.read.parquet(path), .csv, .json and .orc do the same. The default format is Parquet. Readers accept a directory or a glob, so one call can read many files. File sources have defaults worth knowing. CSV reads header=false and inferSchema=false, so every column is a string named _c0, _c1 and so on unless you set header and inferSchema (inference costs an extra pass) or pass a schema. CSV mode is PERMISSIVE by default for corrupt records. JSON expects JSON Lines: each line is one self-contained object, and a regular multi-line JSON file needs option('multiLine', True). All built-in file sources discover partition columns from directory names like country=US and add them as columns. Writes create a directory of part files, one per partition, not a single file; to write one file, reduce to one partition first, accepting the lost parallelism. partitionBy('col') writes a directory per distinct value.

concepts.heading: Reading and Writing with JDBC
concepts.body: The JDBC source reads from and writes to relational databases. You put the driver jar on the classpath and give the url, a table in dbtable or a query in query, and credentials. dbtable accepts anything valid in a FROM clause, so a parenthesized subquery with an alias works; dbtable and query cannot be used together, and query cannot be combined with partitionColumn. By default a JDBC read uses one partition and one connection, so it does not scale. To parallelize, set partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions together; the column must be numeric, date or timestamp. The bounds only decide the stride and do not filter rows, so values outside them still land in the first or last partition. numPartitions also caps concurrent connections, and a write with more partitions than that is coalesced down to the limit. fetchsize (default 0, meaning the driver's own default) sets rows per round trip on reads, and batchsize (default 1000) sets rows per insert batch on writes. Pushdown of filters, aggregates and limits is on by default, so the database does part of the work.

concepts.heading: SQL Directly on Files
concepts.body: You can query a file without loading it into a DataFrame: spark.sql("SELECT * FROM parquet.`/data/users.parquet`"). The format name before the dot (parquet, orc, json, csv, text or delta) selects the data source, and the path goes in backticks. The result is an ordinary DataFrame, so you can keep transforming it. This is convenient for exploration, but it has no schema options: a CSV queried this way uses the source defaults, so column names are _c0, _c1 and so on and values are strings, which is why production code reads with an explicit schema and then registers a view. A path is not a table: it creates no catalog entry, and the next session has to repeat the full path. When the files are partitioned in directories, the partition columns appear in the result and can be used in WHERE to prune directories. The same statement form works for directories of files, not only single files, and Spark still plans the query with Catalyst, so only the needed columns are read from columnar formats such as Parquet and ORC.

concepts.heading: Save Modes
concepts.body: A write checks what already exists at the target before it writes. df.write.mode(...) takes four values. error or errorifexists is the default and throws an exception if data already exists. append adds the new rows to the existing data. overwrite replaces the existing data. ignore silently does nothing if data exists, like CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. The documentation warns that save modes use no locking and are not atomic, and that with overwrite the existing data is deleted before the new data is written, so a failed job can leave the target empty or partial. For a partitioned target, overwrite in the default static mode removes all existing partitions that match the write; setting spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode to dynamic replaces only the partitions that the new data actually contains. A frequent trap is rerunning a job that writes with the default mode: the second run fails because the path already exists. Output committers also vary, so a _SUCCESS marker file is not guaranteed on every store.

examPoints: CSV defaults: no header, no schema inference, all strings; JSON must be JSON Lines unless multiLine is set; writes produce a directory of part files.
JDBC reads use one partition unless partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions are all set; the bounds set the stride and do not filter.
Save modes: errorifexists (default), append, overwrite, ignore; they are neither atomic nor locked, and dynamic partition overwrite replaces only touched partitions.

quiz.q: A job reads a 10-million-row table with spark.read.format('jdbc') using only url, dbtable and credentials. What is the effect on parallelism?
choices: The read uses a single partition and one connection, so setting numPartitions alone does not help without a partition column
Spark splits the table into one partition per 128 MB automatically, using file size estimates
The read uses 200 partitions, the same as spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
Spark opens one connection per executor core, so the load scales with cluster size
quiz.explain: Without partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions the JDBC source reads through one connection into one partition. The 128 MB setting applies to file sources and the shuffle setting to shuffles.

quiz.q: A daily job runs df.write.parquet('/out/sales') with no mode. On the second day the path already holds data. What happens?
choices: The new rows are appended to the existing files
The existing data is replaced by the new data
The write is skipped and the old data stays unchanged
The job fails with an exception because the default mode is errorifexists
quiz.explain: The default save mode throws if data already exists at the target. Append, overwrite and ignore must be requested explicitly with mode().

recap: File readers have documented defaults (CSV strings, JSON Lines, Parquet default format) and writes produce directories of part files. JDBC needs four options together to read in parallel. SQL on files uses format.`path`. Save modes are errorifexists, append, overwrite and ignore, with no atomicity.

title: Persistent Tables with Sorting, Partitioning and Bucketing, and Temporary and Global Temp Views

concepts.heading: Saving to Persistent Tables
concepts.body: df.write.saveAsTable('sales') materializes the DataFrame and registers a pointer to the data in the metastore, so the table survives restarts of the program (as long as the same metastore is used) and spark.table('sales') or SQL can read it later. This is the difference from a temporary view, which stores only a query plan name. If you pass option('path', '/some/path') the table is external: dropping it removes the metadata but leaves the files. Without a path, Spark writes under the warehouse directory and the files are deleted when the table is dropped (a managed table). saveAsTable obeys the same save modes as other writes, so rerunning with the default mode fails when the table exists; overwrite replaces it and append adds rows. Partition information for external tables created with a path is not gathered by default, so MSCK REPAIR TABLE syncs it. The SQL equivalent is CREATE TABLE ... USING parquet AS SELECT .... In both forms the data source format decides the file layout.

concepts.heading: Partitioning, Bucketing and Sorting
concepts.body: Three layout options organize files for faster retrieval. partitionBy('country') writes one directory per distinct value; a filter on that column lets Spark skip whole directories. It works with save and saveAsTable but suits low-cardinality columns, because each distinct value creates a directory and high cardinality produces huge numbers of small files. bucketBy(n, 'col') hashes a column into a fixed number of buckets, so it suits columns with unbounded distinct values, and joins or aggregations on the bucket column can avoid a shuffle when both tables use the same bucketing. sortBy('col') sorts rows inside each bucket. Bucketing and sorting apply only to persistent tables, so bucketBy(...).sortBy(...).save(path) is an error and saveAsTable is required. Partitioning and bucketing can be combined: df.write.partitionBy('c').bucketBy(42, 'k').sortBy('k').saveAsTable('t'). Remember that sortBy on the writer is not a global sort: it orders data only within each bucket file. For a total ordering you need orderBy on the DataFrame before the write, and the writer does not guarantee it will be preserved across files.

concepts.heading: Temporary Views
concepts.body: A temporary view gives a DataFrame a SQL name without writing any data. df.createOrReplaceTempView('t') registers or replaces the name; createTempView('t') raises an error if the name already exists. The view is session-scoped: its lifetime is tied to the SparkSession that created it, it disappears when that session ends, and it is not visible in another session created with newSession(). It holds only the logical plan, so each query on it recomputes from the source unless the underlying DataFrame is cached. spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM t') returns a DataFrame, so SQL and DataFrame code interoperate freely, and you can build a chain of views for readability. A temporary view is not stored in any catalog schema or in the metastore, and no files are created. Views can be dropped with spark.catalog.dropTempView('t'). Registering a view also does not copy or cache data: if the source files change between two queries, the second query can see different rows.

concepts.heading: Global Temporary Views
concepts.body: A global temporary view is shared among all sessions of one Spark application and stays until the application terminates. df.createGlobalTempView('t') creates it in the system-preserved database global_temp, and you must use the qualified name, for example SELECT * FROM global_temp.t; the unqualified name t is not found. spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM global_temp.t') works because the view is cross-session. It does not outlive the application, so a new application or a restart no longer has it. For anything that must outlast the program, use saveAsTable instead. Choosing between the three: a session-scoped need such as breaking a long pipeline into readable SQL steps gets a temporary view; handing a DataFrame to another session in the same application gets a global temporary view; data that other applications must find gets a persistent table. The names also differ in how they fail: createTempView and createGlobalTempView raise an error when the name exists, and the createOrReplace form silently replaces it.

examPoints: saveAsTable registers a persistent table; with a path option it is external (files survive a drop), without it the files are deleted on drop.
partitionBy suits low-cardinality columns; bucketBy and sortBy work only with saveAsTable; sortBy orders within each bucket only.
Temporary view = one session; global temporary view = all sessions of the application, read as global_temp.name; neither survives the application.

quiz.q: A developer runs df.createGlobalTempView('orders') in one session. Which call works from another session of the same application?
choices: spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM orders')
spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM default.orders')
spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM global.orders')
spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM global_temp.orders')
quiz.explain: Global temporary views live in the system database global_temp and must be referenced by the qualified name. An unqualified name only resolves session-scoped views.

quiz.q: Which write statement is valid for sorting rows within buckets and storing the result as a table?
choices: df.write.bucketBy(8, 'id').sortBy('ts').parquet('/out/t')
df.write.bucketBy(8, 'id').sortBy('ts').saveAsTable('t')
df.write.sortBy('ts').saveAsTable('t')
df.write.partitionBy('ts').sortBy('id').parquet('/out/t')
quiz.explain: bucketBy and sortBy apply only to persistent tables, so the write must end in saveAsTable, and sortBy needs bucketBy before it. Direct file writes with those methods fail.

recap: saveAsTable creates catalog tables; a path option makes them external. partitionBy, bucketBy and sortBy have different uses and bucketing needs saveAsTable. A temporary view lives in one session and a global temporary view lives in global_temp for the whole application; createTempView fails on an existing name.
